items.title: Jon Hendricks interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 29, 2000 [interview 2 of 2]
items.q: If it hadn’t been for King Pleasure, for Eddie Jefferson... I would not have had the road sign to point me toward lyricizing orchestral versions of things.

ctx.x: That was my son. Well when you look in jazz history there’s a small number comparatively of real innovators. There’s people that build on the innovations. I think that you’re one of those small number of innovators and gosh, you can take a great deal of pride in that.

Well it’s delicate for me because you must be aware of egoism. Egoism — or is it egotism — I don’t know if there’s a “t” in there or not, and I’m an English major I should know. But anyway you must beware of the ego, the overactivity of the ego. Because man nothing is done alone. If it hadn’t been for King Pleasure, for Eddie Jefferson, for Annie Ross’ “Twisted” and “Farmer’s Market” which were done before Lambert, Hendricks & Ross, I would not have had the road sign to point me toward lyricizing orchestral…

items.title: Jon Hendricks interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, October 18, 1995 [interview 1 of 2]
items.q: Vocalist Jon Hendricks ... has taken the vocalese style of singing pioneered by King Pleasure and Eddie Jefferson to a virtuoso level

ctx.x: Vocalist Jon Hendricks was born in Newark, Ohio in 1921. He has taken the vocalese style of singing pioneered by King Pleasure and Eddie Jefferson to a virtuoso level and is a household name with jazz fans around the world. His unique re-working of Basie standards with Lambert, Hendricks and Ross and later Joe Williams, established a new style of vocal jazz in the late 50s and this trio recorded such classic tunes as “Cloudburst,” “Gimme That Wine” and “Centerpiece.” His production “Evolution of the Blues” became…
Jon was interviewed in New York City by Monk Rowe on October 18, 1995.

items.title: Jon Hendricks — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: I wrote a show called Sing Me a Jazz Song. I had Leon Thomas, Eddie, Annie, and me... But I love Eddie. He was a great person

ctx.x: Whoever that man was that did that. He committed two kinds of murder. He murdered a great step in a cultural art form. That would have been a great thing. We both realized it. Both Eddie and I realized it. He says, “That’s a wonderful thing to do right now.”
So did you have a bond or friendship for any period of time?
